runs.text: Fields with defaults must come after fields without defaults — the same rule as function parameters. If you mix them incorrectly, Python raises TypeError at class-definition time.

For immutable defaults (int, str), just assign them. For mutable defaults (list, dict), use field(default_factory=list) so each new instance gets its own fresh copy — not a shared reference to the class-level object.

cards.title: __post_init__ in Dataclasses
cards.teaser: __post_init__ is the hook dataclasses call after the generated __init__ sets all fields — the right place for derived fields, cross-field validation, and any setup logic that depends on multiple inputs.

A common pattern is marking computed fields with

— compute and assign attributes that depend on other fields.
— convert string inputs to enums, decimals, or domain objects.

runs.text: With frozen=True, __post_init__ cannot use self.x = ... directly — frozen dataclasses block normal attribute assignment after __init__. Use object.__setattr__(self, 'x', value) instead, which bypasses the frozen guard only during construction.

__post_init__ is the "after the fields are set" hook. Think of it as the custom part of the constructor — the generated __init__ handles the mechanical field-setting, and __post_init__ handles everything that requires thought.

cards.title: Immutability with frozen=True
cards.teaser: @dataclass(frozen=True) makes every field read-only after construction — assignment raises FrozenInstanceError, and the instance becomes hashable so it can be used in sets and as dict keys.

Frozen dataclasses are the Pythonic way to model value objects — things like coordinates, currency amounts, or configuration keys that should never change once created.

runs.text: If you need a mutable working copy before "locking in" a value, build with a regular dataclass and convert to a frozen version in a factory method that returns replace(instance). This pattern mirrors the builder pattern from other languages.

frozen=True turns a dataclass into a read-only record. Once created, you can't change any field — Python will raise an error. As a bonus, it becomes hashable: you can put it in a set or use it as a dict key.

cards.title: collections.namedtuple
cards.teaser: namedtuple creates a tuple subclass with named fields — giving tuple's immutability and positional access with the readability of attribute names, at essentially no memory overhead over a plain tuple.

runs.text: conveys nothing about what the first element represents.
produces a tuple subclass with named positions:
are as readable as attributes while remaining positionally indexable and iterable.
Namedtuples are immutable — you cannot assign to their fields after creation. They also inherit all tuple behaviors: unpacking, slicing,

— converts to an ordered dict, handy for serialization.

runs.text: namedtuple has no type annotations on its fields — all fields are untyped from the static-analysis perspective. For typed named records, prefer typing.NamedTuple (see next card) which supports full annotations and mypy integration.
A namedtuple is a tuple where every slot has a name. You get all the compactness of a tuple — immutable, iterable, hashable — plus the readability of dot-notation attributes like p.x and p.y.

cards.title: typing.NamedTuple
cards.teaser: typing.NamedTuple is the class-based, typed alternative to collections.namedtuple — it supports field annotations, default values, and regular method definitions, while remaining a true tuple subclass.

runs.text: lets you write a class with annotations:

class Point(NamedTuple):
    x: float
    y: float
    label: str = ''
This form is strictly more capable than
: fields are annotated (so mypy understands them), default values are allowed (fields with defaults must come last), and you can add regular methods to the class body.

items.text: ; positional indexing, unpacking, and hashing all work.
— define computed properties and helper methods in the class body; they coexist with tuple mechanics.

runs.text: Prefer typing.NamedTuple over collections.namedtuple in all new code. The class syntax is more readable, integrates with mypy, and supports defaults without the verbose _field_defaults workaround.

typing.NamedTuple is collections.namedtuple with type annotations and a nicer syntax. You write it like a class, you get type-checked immutable records, and it still behaves exactly like a tuple under the hood.

cards.title: typing.TypedDict
cards.teaser: TypedDict defines a dictionary schema with per-key type annotations — letting mypy check that you're not misspelling keys or storing the wrong type, while the runtime object is still a plain dict.

runs.text: — the type checker knows the keys are strings and the values can be anything, but it cannot validate individual keys.
narrows this: you declare exactly which keys exist and what type each holds, and mypy treats each key access as typed.
TypedDict is purely a static-analysis construct — at runtime, the object is an ordinary
. There is no class instantiation overhead, no validation at runtime, and no extra memory usage. It is a contract enforced by the type checker, not the interpreter.

items.text: — makes all keys optional; combine with inheritance to split required and optional keys into separate TypedDicts.
(Python 3.11+) — mark individual keys as optional within a total=True TypedDict, without needing two classes.
— TypedDict is ideal for JSON API response shapes that arrive as dicts but have a known structure.

runs.text: TypedDict does not validate at runtime. If an external source (an API, a config file) sends the wrong type for a key, Python won't raise an error — the type checker only catches mistakes in your own code. Use pydantic or dataclasses with __post_init__ when runtime validation is required.

TypedDict tells the type checker "this dict always has these specific keys with these specific types." At runtime it's just a plain dict — no overhead, no validation. The benefit is entirely in your editor and mypy catching typos and type mismatches before you run the code.

cards.title: Dataclass vs NamedTuple vs dict: When to Pick Which
cards.teaser: Use a dataclass for mutable value types with behavior; NamedTuple for immutable lightweight records that need to behave as tuples; TypedDict or plain dict when the shape must remain a dictionary for interop.

runs.text: Python offers four main ways to group related data — plain
— and the right choice depends on mutability, behavior, and interop requirements.

items.text: — when the data must stay a dict for JSON serialization, **kwargs passing, or interop with APIs that expect dicts. TypedDict adds type-checker coverage without changing the runtime type.
— when you want a lightweight, immutable record that participates in tuple protocols (unpacking, positional indexing, CSV-style iteration). Low overhead, naturally hashable.
— when you want a first-class object with methods, inheritance, optional mutability, computed fields, and full control over construction. The general-purpose choice for domain objects.
— when you need the capabilities of a dataclass but also immutability and hashability. Prefer this over NamedTuple when the tuple protocol is not needed.

runs.text: Rule of thumb: start with @dataclass. Move to NamedTuple if you specifically need tuple behavior (positional indexing, CSV unpacking). Move to TypedDict only when the data must remain a plain dict.

dict is for data that must stay a dictionary. NamedTuple is for compact read-only records that behave like tuples. dataclass is for full domain objects with methods and optional mutability. When in doubt, start with dataclass.

cards.title: __slots__ for Memory-Efficient Instances
cards.teaser: __slots__ replaces the per-instance __dict__ with a fixed-size array of slots — cutting per-instance memory significantly and slightly speeding up attribute access, at the cost of flexibility.

— attribute access is marginally faster (array lookup vs dict lookup).

runs.text: Apply __slots__ only when profiling shows per-instance memory is a bottleneck. It adds friction (no dynamic attributes, inheritance complications) that rarely pays off for typical business objects with fewer than 10,000 live instances.

__slots__ is a promise: "this class only ever needs these exact attributes." In exchange for that promise, Python drops the per-instance dictionary and uses a lean fixed-size array — saving significant memory when you have millions of instances.

cards.title: Dataclass Inheritance
cards.teaser: Dataclasses support inheritance — the child class inherits parent fields and generated methods, with child fields appended after parent fields in __init__. One key rule: parent fields with defaults must not precede child fields without defaults.

runs.text: takes all parent fields (in declaration order) followed by the child's own fields.
similarly cover all fields from both.

The ordering constraint matters: if the parent has a field with a default value, then every subsequent field in the child must also have a default — because Python cannot put a required parameter after an optional one. This can be surprising when you extend a base class that already has some defaults.

items.text: — a child can redeclare a parent field with a different default; the child's version wins.
— a non-frozen child cannot inherit from a frozen parent (TypeError). Both must be frozen or both non-frozen.
(Python 3.10+) to force fields after it to be keyword-only, sidestepping ordering conflicts.

runs.text: Deep dataclass hierarchies often signal a design problem. If you find yourself stacking three or four layers of @dataclass inheritance, consider composition instead — a field that holds an instance of the parent type, rather than inheriting from it.

When a dataclass inherits from another, the child's __init__ lists all the parent's fields first, then the child's own. The main gotcha: if the parent has any default-valued fields, all child fields must also have defaults — you can't put a required argument after an optional one.

cards.title: Performance: dataclass vs dict vs __slots__
cards.teaser: Plain dicts have lower creation overhead for small structures; dataclasses add a negligible layer; __slots__ cuts per-instance memory by roughly half. Measure before optimizing — the difference rarely matters below 100,000 instances.

runs.text: Performance comparisons among Python's structured data options depend on workload:

items.text: literal creation is fastest (the interpreter has a specialized opcode). A dataclass constructor is comparable to a handwritten
. NamedTuple creation is slightly slower (tuple allocation + field assignment).
uses ~400 bytes overhead; a slotted class drops that to ~50–100 bytes. A NamedTuple (tuple subclass) is the most compact: only the tuple header plus one pointer per field.
— slots access is marginally faster than dict-backed attribute access because it skips the hash lookup.
— Python 3.10+ combines dataclass convenience with slot memory savings, making it the best default when memory matters.

runs.text: In practice, structural choice should be driven by semantics (mutability, behavior, interop) first. Only optimize for performance after measuring with

If you're storing millions of homogeneous records — sensor readings, log events, coordinate pairs — consider numpy structured arrays or pandas DataFrames, which store data in contiguous C arrays and are orders of magnitude more memory-efficient than any Python object approach.

The memory hierarchy from most to least compact is: NamedTuple (smallest) > slotted dataclass > regular dataclass > dict. For most applications the difference is undetectable. Profile first, then reach for __slots__ or @dataclass(slots=True) only if memory is actually tight.
